title: Cloning players, hating on TEs and who has most to prove? Panthers mailbag Young needs to build on a solid 2025 and Brooks needs to have a healthy season. Also, what's the deal at nickel? Joseph Person 2
summary:

CHARLOTTE, N.C. — As the slow drip of the NFL schedule release proceeds before Thursday’s gush of the full 18-week slate, it felt like an opportune time to make the callout for Carolina Panthers’ questions.
Readers were most curious about Bryce Young’s future as the quarterback heads into an important season, but al
full_text:
Panther GM Dan Morgan picked up the fifth-year option on QB Bryce Young, but no decision has been made on an extension for the 2023 No. 1 overall pick. Jared C. Tilton / Getty Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — As the slow drip of the NFL schedule release proceeds before Thursday’s gush of the full 18-week slate, it felt like an opportune time to make the callout for Carolina Panthers’ questions.
Readers were most curious about Bryce Young’s future as the quarterback heads into an important season, but also asked about topics ranging from Xavier Legette and Jonathon Brooks to the team’s draft and, naturally, tight ends.
There were no questions about the Panthers’ schedule, despite Roger Goodell’s insistence on turning it into a weeklong event. That might have something to do with the fact that fans have known their teams’ opponents since January.
At any rate, let’s get to questions, some of which have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Is this a prove-it camp for Jonathon Brooks? No one has discussed the possibility of him getting cut and joining the practice squad. — Micah T.
Heading into training camp, who has the most to prove? (Legette) is high on the list, but it feels like Trevin Wallace has been shown a lot of trust, Chuba (Hubbard) is back to being primary after (Rico) Dowdle, Brooks will be trying to prove himself, and Bryce will have something to prove. — David S.
You could make a case for each of those players having the most riding on the 2026 season. Viewed strictly through a financial lens, no one stands to gain or lose more money than Bryce Young, who is entering the fourth year of his rookie deal. The Panthers exercised Young’s fifth-year option at $26.5 million for 2027, and aren’t expected to extend the No. 1 pick from 2023 before this season.
Two NFL talent evaluators told The Athletic in January that a Young extension should average about $33 million annually, matching the current deals of ex-Carolina QBs Baker Mayfield and Sam Darnold. That’s well below the $46 million AAV that Kyler Murray — another No. 1 pick — received from the Arizona Cardinals in 2022, after Murray had led Arizona to the playoffs and had gone to back-to-back Pro Bowls. Murray was the Offensive Rookie of the Year in 2019.
As for the other prove-it guys, Legette leads the list of players who enter the season on shaky ground. Chris Brazzell II, the third-round pick from Tennessee, has a similar size-speed profile to Legette and looked the part during rookie minicamp. Still, running against air is a lot different than facing Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson in training camp, and Brazzell’s transition could include a few bumps due to his limited route tree at Tennessee.
Nose tackle Bobby Brown is another veteran who needs to step up or risk losing his spot to a rookie. Brown was mostly a non-factor after signing a three-year, $21 million deal in 2025, and now has second-round pick Lee Hunter to contend with.
Brooks has the most to prove physically as he attempts to come back from a second ACL surgery on his right knee. To Micah’s question, it wouldn’t make sense to cut Brooks while he’s still on a rookie deal with manageable cap hits the next two years.
Despite spending quite a lot of time in the appropriate formation, it feels like the Panthers don’t have a nailed-on starter at nickel and didn’t sign or draft an obvious challenger to Chau Smith-Wade. Do you think there’s a candidate for the job on the roster — Zakee Wheatley, maybe? Or do you think that the coaches and GM just don’t view it as being that much of an issue? — Matthew G.
Good question, and one that allows me to touch on Wheatley, a player I didn’t write much about during the draft or rookie minicamp. To Matthew’s point, I don’t think the Panthers viewed nickel corner as a huge priority because they still have Smith-Wade under contract, as well as Corey Thornton, who Canales said had taken the spot before his rookie season ended with a broken fibula in late November.
“We have Chau coming back. We have Corey Thornton, who really won the job during the season last year and got an opportunity until he got hurt,” Canales said after the second rookie camp practice. “So there’s a great competition already happening.”
The Panthers look for length and versatility on defense. The 6-1, 195-pound Thornton has both, showing he could play inside and outside after the Panthers signed him as an undrafted free agent from Louisville. The same is true of rookie corner DeVonta Smith, another UDFA who spent a lot of time in the slot last year at Notre Dame but also can play outside.
As for Wheatley, Morgan indicated the fifth-rounder’s versatility is more about his ability to play both safety spots than getting in the mix at nickel.
“Just a big, long, physical guy. He fits the DNA that we want, the type of competitor we want,” Morgan said of the Penn State product. “He can play in the post. He can play up in the box. He can do a lot of things for our defense that we’re excited about.”
The public Dillon Thieneman hype was real. Did you ever get a sense that the Panthers were high on him? Was he the pick if (Monroe) Freeling was off the board? — Jlc 3
The Panthers were more interested in Thieneman than tight end Kenyon Sadiq, his Oregon teammate, who was also a popular pick for Carolina at 19 in mock drafts. The priority was offensive tackle, with Freeling and Alabama’s Kadyn Proctor, who went 12th to the Miami Dolphins, the most realistic targets. The Panthers liked both players, although Freeling’s athleticism and upside seemingly gave him an edge over Proctor, who will begin his Dolphins’ career as a guard.
Thieneman’s speed and ball skills would have looked good at the back end of Ejiro Evero’s defense, but Morgan, who has a history of doubling up at certain positions, wanted to get younger (and cheaper) along the offensive line after not drafting an O-lineman his first two years as GM.
With Brad Idzik taking over play-call duties, what do you think the biggest change will be? Are there any noted differences in opinion and philosophy between Dave (Canales) and Brad or do you expect the scheme to carry on exactly as it was? — Matt J.
Canales and Idzik are very close. When Canales was preparing to interview for the Baltimore Ravens’ offensive coordinator position a few years ago, Idzik stayed up late cramming with Canales as he fine-tuned his vision for the scheme he would run when he became a play caller. I’d be surprised if there’s a major shift in scheme.
Idzik alluded to that collaboration after Canales announced in February he was handing off the play-calling duties. “It seems like a big change, but it really isn’t because I’ve been alongside of him the whole step of the way of his growth, and being an offensive coordinator from Tampa to here,” Idzik said. “That part’s been fun, pinging ideas off each other, learning from his experiences.”
Idzik can put his own spin on things on Sundays. Every play caller develops his own rhythm and feel for calling the offense, and the 34-year-old Idzik is no different. The other piece of the play-calling picture is Darrell Bevell, the former Seattle Seahawks offensive coordinator who joined Canales’ staff in February. Canales has said the 56-year-old Bevell will be a “big part” of the offensive process and serve as an experienced voice whom Idzik can lean on.
Moving on to the speed round …
Any chance that Haynes King unseats Kenny Pickett as Bryce’s backup? — Jensen H.
Probably not. But King getting the nod for QB3 over Will Grier, joining the practice squad and running the opposing team’s offense could definitely happen.
With OT having a pretty clear top 3 of Moton, Freeling and Walker, who do you see being our interior OL — Lewis, Hunt, Fortner, Hecht and Zavala? Other? — William P.
I think you pretty much nailed it, William. Except for Other. Not enough position versatility, so he’s not on my depth chart. It’s also probably worth keeping an eye on Nick Samac. The Ravens’ seventh-round…

full_text:
Stanford grad Sam Roush has the smarts and bloodlines to succeed in the NFL. "Football's in my blood, and that's a big part of who I am," he says. Kamil Krzaczynski / Imagn Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — On a play against BYU, Sam Roush had an assignment to chip the defensive end.
A chip block is normally a quick jolt just to slow down a defensive player, but the Chicago Bears’ third-round pick did more than that.
Roush blocked the defensive end so hard that he knocked him into the defensive tackle, and both players went to the ground.
“He pancaked two guys in one play,” Stanford tight ends coach Nate Byham told The Athletic . “He hit the guy square, rolled his hips, snapped through him and sent him launching into a 300-and-some-pound D-lineman and knocked him over as well.”
We learned this year about what Bears head coach Ben Johnson is like when he watches film of players who play his style of football. Assistant director of college scouting Francis St. Paul described Johnson as rocking back and forth.
Roush’s double-pancake block probably caught Johnson’s eye.
“He’s a finisher through the whistle, and I think that showed up on a consistent basis,” Johnson said of Roush after the draft. “It didn’t matter who he was blocking — could be a big guy, could be a little DB, and he consistently finished through the whistle each and every play. You always love it when you take a player and you get a text message from somebody.
“One of his coaches at Stanford said he will crush himself to do whatever he can to help the football team. And it just verifies what you already thought about the player. So feel good about that one.”
That sure sounds like a Ben Johnson player, and with the league starting to move to more three-tight-end sets — “13 personnel” — Roush seemed like a Johnson pick at No. 69. When many expected a defensive lineman to be the choice, Roush might have been the most surprising pick, as he joins a tight ends room with last year’s 10th overall pick (Colston Loveland) and Cole Kmet, a second-rounder in 2020.
But when you learn more about Roush and what the Bears want to do, it makes a lot of sense.
The first thing Roush looked at when he opened his Bears playbook? The formations.
“I’ve been told when you’re learning a new playbook, you want to start with formations and then you can kind of go into motions and shifts and learn all that,” he said Friday after his first Bears practice. “With the formations there comes the splits. Once you get to that point, I learn the runs first and then the passing concepts. And then a lot of times with the run plays or the pass concepts, the splits will change. So you can learn those nuances after you’ve learned the base rules. But I think just kind of a ground-up approach is how you should do it.”
He sounds like someone who graduated with a 3.8 GPA from Stanford and a degree in computer science.
“He is a very impressive young man,” Johnson said. “Obviously, you go to a school like that and take education seriously like he has, he’s very bright. I don’t think he’ll have any problem picking up the details with which we like to play.”
At Stanford, Roush had to learn three different offenses — David Shaw’s pro-style system, Troy Taylor’s air-raid college system and then Frank Reich and Byham’s pro-style scheme in 2025.
Byham tallied a grand total of one mental error for Roush all season.
Roush has the smarts and the bloodlines. His dad played defensive back at Duke. His mom played volleyball at Montana State. His mom’s father is Phil Olsen, who spent six seasons in the NFL as a defensive tackle. Roush’s maternal uncle? Merlin Olsen, a 14-time Pro Bowler and a Hall of Famer.
“Football’s in my blood, and that’s a big part of who I am,” he said, “and I always knew it was something I was gonna do.”
A traditional Y tight end; will do a blocker’s dirty work with underneath receiving upside.
Out of 319 prospects at the NFL combine, Roush was one of six to compete in every drill.
“I love to compete,” he said. “I was telling coaches all week I was going to do everything and I didn’t even know people were going to skip out on stuff until right up until the end, after we did all our drill work. I was like, ‘I’m not going to skip out on the shuttle.’
“I get to do it once in my lifetime, so I felt like I could take advantage of it.”
According to the Relative Athletic Score database , Roush scored in the 99th percentile for tight ends dating to 1987, ranking 10th out of 1,471 tight ends.
Athletic? Check. Strength to block? Check. Agility and a quick 10-yard split? Check and check.
“He has so much explosion through his lower body that a lot of guys just do not have, especially at that size,” Byham said. “You look at the combine numbers, I think it was a 10-5 broad jump. … But you can just see the raw power that he can generate at that size, and that’s all blocking is, it’s hip mobility and that explosion, and he has that, which makes him different, because most blocking tight ends might be 6-6, 265 pounds, but they don’t have that step.”
Byham was a sixth-round pick in the ultimate tight ends draft, 2010, when 19 tight ends were selected, including Rob Gronkowski, Jimmy Graham and Roush’s position coach, Jim Dray.
Like Roush, the strongest part of Byham’s scouting report was his ability to block. But in 16 years, we’re seeing the league go through another cycle.
Twenty-two tight ends were drafted last month. Roush was the sixth to go, as teams used Day 2 to find their “Y” tight ends to prepare for multiple-tight-end formations.
“Things always go full circle, it seems like,” Johnson said. “It wasn’t that long ago that three-receiver sets were kind of the norm, and now it seems to be transitioning a little bit more. But I think the more you can look to attack the defense, whether you want to give them a base defense or you feel comfortable competing against them when they’re in their sub defenses, the flexibility that tight ends give you, I think it adds a dimension to your offense.”
On one of the most memorable plays in Bears regular-season history, three tight ends stood in the huddle — Kmet, Loveland and Durham Smythe — in a Week 16 home game against the Green Bay Packers.
Smythe, the team’s No. 3 tight end, was able to redirect Packers linebacker Quay Walker just enough to give quarterback Caleb Williams the time to find receiver DJ Moore for the game-winning touchdown in overtime.
A few weeks later, with the Bears trailing by 5 points in the wild-card playoff game, Johnson flexed both arms over his head, a signal for a jumbo formation. The three tight ends headed out to the field for a 2-point conversion. Williams then audibled, and Loveland was split out wide against a Packers linebacker. He won the matchup and caught the 2-pointer en route to the comeback win.
With less than seven minutes to go on “Black Friday,” the Bears led the Philadelphia Eagles 17-9. They had attacked Philadelphia all afternoon with their running backs and seemed poised to do so again when they exited the huddle with three tight ends on second-and-8. Williams faked a handoff to running back D’Andre Swift before drifting to his left and floating a touchdown pass to Kmet to seal what was a signature win.
Three of the biggest plays of the Bears’ magical season took place in “13 personnel.” Smythe signed with the Baltimore Ravens this offseason, creating a hole, one that we didn’t expect to be filled with a premium pick in the top 70.
But this is where the NFL is going .
“For a team that runs a lot of ’12’ and ’13 personnel,’” general manager Ryan Poles said on draft night, “I think we were top five in both those personnel groups, that was important for us to add a ‘Y’ to that group so we’ll have a really strong room.”
In 2025, the Bears ran 32.5 percent of their plays in “12 personnel,” tied for the sixth-highest rate in the league. They were in “13” for 8.5 percent of snaps, fifth most.

full_text:
Broncos fourth-round pick Kage Casey was an All-American left tackle at Boise State, but he has a chance to become Denver's left guard of the future if he can master a slide inside. Tyler McFarland / Getty Images
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — Amid the swirl of hugs, smiles and celebratory yells, Kage Casey felt his phone buzz. It was a FaceTime request. He didn’t recognize the number.
“I was a little scared to pick it up,” said Casey, the offensive lineman from Boise State who received the call minutes after being selected by the Denver Broncos in the fourth round of last month’s NFL Draft.
Casey ultimately accepted the call and immediately saw the wide-grinning Garett Bolles, Denver’s veteran left tackle. The call added a touch of surreality to a whirlwind day for Casey. As a three-year starter at left tackle for Boise State, the 6-foot-5, 310-pounder said he studied Bolles closely, trying to mimic aspects of how last year’s first-team All-Pro for the Broncos plied his craft.
“He’s helped me a lot ever since (that first call),” Casey said.
The fourth-round pick the Broncos used on the 22-year-old Casey represented the biggest investment of draft capital they’ve spent on an offensive lineman since the team selected guard Quinn Meinerz, another first-team All-Pro last season, in the third round of the 2021 draft. The question now is whether Casey will ultimately line up next to his new mentor on the left side of Denver’s offensive line.
“I’m ready to learn wherever I need to be,” he said.
Casey, who started 41 straight games at left tackle across his final three seasons at Boise State, lined up at left guard during the Broncos’ rookie minicamp last week. It was an early clue for how Denver could develop its newest piece on the offensive line for coaches Zach Strief and Chris Morgan. It’s early, of course. Depth charts and firm roster decisions are months away. Casey figures to get looks across the line in the offseason practices to come.
“He’s got flex (capabilities),” Broncos coach Sean Payton said of Casey. “He is one of those guys who we felt could do a lot and even go inside and play center.”
The sight of Casey at left guard during the earliest stages of the offseason was nonetheless notable given the uncertainty that exists at the position beyond the upcoming season.
Veteran starter Ben Powers is entering the final year of the contract he signed with the Broncos as a free agent in 2023. Casey could be a candidate to step into the starting lineup by next season if Powers leaves as a free agent. Alex Palczewski, who filled in as the starter at left guard during most of Powers’ nine-game injury absence last year, will also be under contract in 2027 after signing a two-year extension in March. The Broncos have enjoyed veteran continuity on the offensive line for much of Payton’s tenure as head coach, dating back to 2023, but they’ve also intentionally added and developed depth — mostly by way of late-round picks and undrafted free agents — during that same time period.
The latest example is Casey, who represents an important step in Denver’s plan to build a sustainable offensive line room. The Broncos are set to spend $93.7 million on their offensive line, according to Spotrac, just a shade below the Carolina Panthers for the most in that league. Making that unit more cost-effective in future years will be crucial as the franchise prepares for an eventual massive contract for quarterback Bo Nix.
It all makes Casey’s development one of the more intriguing subplots for the Broncos during the next year.
“Through his whole process, I was like, ‘Hey, Kage is going to be a good player,'” said his position coach at Boise State, Tim Keane. “He’s a no-brainer. He’s a professional right now. He’s organized and has designed his life to excel at football. But I was like, ‘If he gets into the right place and the right organization, he could be a great player. I think he’s found the right organization that is going to allow him to flourish and grow and be the best version of himself.”
Keane’s first impression of Casey came during the summer of 2021. The COVID-19 pandemic was still limiting recruiting outreach for colleges. Assistants weren’t yet back on the road canvassing the country to meet with prospective players, but schools were given the green light to host recruits for staggered workouts on campus.
The first player to work out for the Boise State staff was a running back named Ashton Jeanty, who later became a first-round pick of the Las Vegas Raiders less than four years later.
“The very next guy — because you can only work out one guy at a time — was Kage Casey,” said Keane, who has coached at Boise State since January of 2021. “He did about two minutes of his workout and we’re like, ‘Oh my gosh, this guy has really high upside, huge potential.’ The thing we try to do really hard here is make sure he’s wired the right way and make sure he’s a big culture guy to fit our locker room and our DNA. Once we checked the physical box, we started the long process of making sure he’s going to be a fit in the locker room. … He was a definite fit.”
Casey arrived at Boise by way of Happy Valley, Ore., during the spring semester in 2022. He weighed only 250 pounds and knew his top priority as a freshman would be to gain weight. It was how he went about that process that gave Boise State’s staff the first inclination they were working with a special player.
“He’s willing to do all the things that are not glamorous and that people don’t recognize or applaud you for,” Keane said. “He was willing, for his first two years of college, to get up at 5 a.m. and make himself a pound of ground turkey and a cup of rice and eat that before his 6 a.m. workout because he’s trying to gain weight — the good weight. We don’t have lavish cafeterias or any of those things, so it was like, ‘Hey, we can put a plan in place, but you have to work the plan,’ and that’s exactly what he did. He was committed to being the best possible offensive lineman he could be.”
Casey, Keane noted, is not “a genetic lottery winner.” He isn’t 6-foot-7. He’s not “freaky long or freaky athletic.”
“He separates himself by being a master of his craft and being a master of his technique, understanding the game at a really, really elite level,” Keane said. “That’s where he’s kind of been able to develop and grow to a really unique player.”
That has become a requirement to join the development pipeline that feeds Denver’s offensive front. Payton, Strief said earlier this year, has always sought offensive linemen who are “smart, tough (and) who endear themselves to teammates.” Strief said he can spend the majority of practices helping linemen develop and sharpen their techniques because the Broncos add players into the room who can quickly grasp their responsibilities within the team’s concepts.
“We talk a lot about spending as much time as we can on technique — more than who you’re blocking,” Strief said. “We’re not walking through blocking schemes out here (on the practice field). We’re not going to do it because we need time for that other stuff. When we got together initially (as a coaching staff in 2023), the real conversation was about being intentional.”
The other hallmark of Denver’s developmental program has become versatility, highlighted by Palczewski’s jump last season from right tackle to left guard. Casey was a second-team All-American at left tackle while playing for Boise State, helping to pave the way for Jeanty’s 2024 campaign that saw him rush for 2,601 yards, the second-most in FBS history. But Casey never balked at the idea of potentially moving to a new position as the pre-draft process began for him earlier this year.
“To be honest, my ego was hurt more than his ego,” Keane said. “I’m like, ‘What are you talking about? This guy is an All-American tackle.'”
Casey spent the two weeks before his pro day in late March learning how to snap for the first time.
“Someone told me that’s what they want me to…

title: The Lions' offseason winners and losers: Many reasons for Jared Goff to be happy A new offensive coordinator and pass game coordinator, plus a first-round tackle and free-agent center are reasons for Goff to smile. Colton Pouncy 1
summary:
Jared Goff watched the Lions strengthen their O-line in free agency and the draft. Junfu Han / Imagn Images
The bulk of the work in free agency is complete. The 2026 NFL Draft is over. And the Detroit Lions are ready to roll.

full_text:
Jared Goff watched the Lions strengthen their O-line in free agency and the draft. Junfu Han / Imagn Images
The bulk of the work in free agency is complete. The 2026 NFL Draft is over. And the Detroit Lions are ready to roll.
It’s been an offseason of righting wrongs, and the Lions are hoping their work yields desired results when the season kicks off in September. But before then, which players are set up for success in 2026? Which ones have work to do after the Lions rounded out their roster?
Let’s take a look at some offseason winners and losers.
There might not be a happier soul at the Meijer Performance Center than Jared Goff. Think about what the Lions got him this offseason.
• An offensive coordinator co-signed by Ben Johnson and viewed as a detail-oriented and adaptable mind.
• A former NFL QB, OC and interim head coach, Mike Kafka, to be his passing game coordinator.
• A new starting center, starting left tackle, first-round right tackle and added depth along the offensive line.
• An experienced backup QB and friend in Teddy Bridgewater.
Goff performed well under less-than-ideal circumstances last season, to the tune of 4,564 yards, 34 passing touchdowns and just eight interceptions. He’s not a player worth worrying about, but additions to the coaching staff and along the offensive line should only aid Goff as he enters Year 6 in Detroit and Year 11 overall.
Terrion Arnold showed improvement in his second season. When targeted in man coverage, Arnold allowed just 9.5 yards per reception (17th fewest among qualified CBs), a passer rating of 77.1 (36th). Not mind-blowing statistics, but enough to warrant patience as he navigates life as a young NFL cornerback. However, after an injury-plagued 2025 season and offseason in the headlines for all the wrong reasons , is patience running thin?
“I need him to be quiet and just play,” Lions DC Kelvin Sheppard said of Arnold at the NFL Combine. “He wants to be great, but I told him (there’s) a difference between talking about being great and actually being great, and he’s starting to understand that.”
That sent a message that this would be an important offseason for Arnold — a confident player whose game is still catching up to his bravado. Those strides Arnold made were accompanied by a wave of nagging injuries and a subsequent shoulder surgery. In total, he played in just eight games last season.
In the weeks that followed Sheppard’s comments, Arnold’s name was linked to an armed robbery and kidnapping that took place in Florida this offseason. Arnold has not been charged and his attorney denies his involvement, but it’s a situation worth monitoring in the event things change. It’s not the sort of news you hope to read about your 2024 first-round pick who is still trying to live up to his draft stock.
If Arnold’s off-field situation doesn’t escalate and he can focus on football, this could be the year he puts it all together. But as Sheppard said, there’s a difference between talking about being great and actually being great.
An obvious one here, but the Lions and Blake Miller were a perfect match for a number of reasons. The team has been open about moving Penei Sewell to left tackle, which would create a hole at right tackle. To fill it, the Lions grabbed arguably the most NFL-ready right tackle in the class in Miller — a 6-foot-7, 317-pound lineman with 54 career starts in college and a relative athletic score of 9.90. As a high-character, selfless prospect, Miller should fit into the locker room seamlessly. If all goes according to plan, the Lions might not be picking this high again in the future, so locking in Miller as their right tackle of the future felt like the best course of action at No. 17. His future looks bright.
Has the physical traits, football IQ and toughness that NFL teams will bet on every time.
In an ideal world, the Lions would’ve seen enough from Giovanni Manu over the last two seasons to feel comfortable naming him a starter in 2026. It would’ve allowed them to move on from Taylor Decker and have a replacement, in the third year of his rookie contract, ready to go. Manu’s upside was undeniable, and when you reach Day 3 of the draft, it’s fair to take swings if the conviction is there. The price was high, though, requiring a 2025 third-round pick to secure him in the fourth round of the 2024 NFL Draft. But now that the dust has settled, it’s clear the Lions didn’t believe Manu was ready, which paved the way for Miller. Manu at best looks like OT4 heading into his third NFL season, slotting behind Sewell, Miller and Larry Borom. There’s still hope that things can click for him, but the Lions are set at tackle for the foreseeable future.
As expected, the Lions and veteran defensive tackle DJ Reader went their separate ways this offseason. Reader officially signed with the New York Giants earlier this month. When the Lions drafted Tyleik Williams in the first round in 2025, this felt like a foregone conclusion. Williams, a cerebral nose tackle who’s light on his feet for a player of his stature, is the future of the position. He flashed as a rookie and has the goods to be a long-term starter opposite Alim McNeill. Both players are under contract for the next three seasons, and their games complement each other well. If McNeill returns to his pre-ACL form and Williams takes a Year 2 leap, they could form one of the better defensive interiors in football.
With Kalif Raymond signing with the Bears this offseason, an opportunity arose for Dominic Lovett. A 2025 seventh-round pick, Lovett was drafted for his gadget potential on offense and potential special teams contributions. However, the Lions quickly replaced Raymond with Greg Dortch, then traded up for Kentucky receiver Kendrick Law in the fifth round of the draft. There’s quite a bit of overlap between those players, and considering Lovett wasn’t a roster lock as a rookie, he’ll need to really prove his value this summer to make the team.
This one could’ve been filed either way. Technically, Christian Mahogany will have to earn his job this year, in ways he didn’t have to a year ago. He’ll have to fend off both Miles Frazier and veteran Ben Bartch at left guard. But the added competition and moves made around him could give him the inside track.
Outside of Goff, Mahogany should benefit the most from Sewell’s move from right tackle to left. Sewell has a chance to elevate Mahogany’s game as a natural people mover with the physical prowess to win his own one-on-one and help out the man next to him. Mahogany spent the 2025 season next to an injured left tackle in Decker and a rapidly declining Graham Glasgow at center. Now he gets Sewell and an ascending center in Cade Mays. If the Lions implement more gap looks into their run game under offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, it could also benefit a player like Mahogany, whose game is more power than athleticism.
Mahogany is a bit of a wild card. He played poorly in his first year as a starter, was injured and lacks pedigree as a sixth-round pick. But the Lions have seemingly positioned him for a breakout, should he be ready for one, while hedging with solid options in Bartch and Frazier. It looks like it’s Mahogany’s job to lose.
A 2024 second-round pick, Ennis Rakestraw had an excellent training camp as a rookie and once looked like he could push for a starting job at nickel. He told reporters at the end of his rookie season that the coaching staff was prepping him to start at nickel in Week 2 of the 2024 season, before a hamstring injury suffered during pregame warm-ups ruined those plans. Rakestraw spent much of the year on injured reserve, as Amik Robertson cemented himself as a starter.
Since then, Rakestraw’s career has been derailed by injuries. As the 2025 offseason unfolded, the front office couldn’t count on him to start as an outside cornerback, so they signed Reed. Rakestraw would go on to miss the entire 2025 season with a shoulder injury that required surgery. While…

title: Colts post-draft mailbag: Who would start at QB in Week 1 if Daniel Jones can't? What's the plan at wide receiver, which players entering contract years are in line for extensions and more in our post-draft mailbag. James Boyd 3
summary:
The Colts could have a backup quarterback competition this summer between Anthony Richardson Sr., left, and Riley Leonard, right, behind starter Daniel Jones, center. Mykal McEldowney / IndyStar / USA Today Network via Imagn Images
Anthony Richardson Sr. is back, Kenny Moore II is gone and the Indianapolis Colts’ roster (for the most part) appears to be set after the NFL Draft. Amid a pivotal offseason filled with change, I asked you all to weigh in about the state of the franchise. Let’s dive i
full_text:
The Colts could have a backup quarterback competition this summer between Anthony Richardson Sr., left, and Riley Leonard, right, behind starter Daniel Jones, center. Mykal McEldowney / IndyStar / USA Today Network via Imagn Images
Anthony Richardson Sr. is back, Kenny Moore II is gone and the Indianapolis Colts’ roster (for the most part) appears to be set after the NFL Draft. Amid a pivotal offseason filled with change, I asked you all to weigh in about the state of the franchise. Let’s dive into your questions in my first post-draft mailbag!
Is there a chance Richardson is waived? It’s clear the coaching staff wants nothing to do with him. — Anonymous U.
Before Richardson rejoined the Colts for spring practice, I honestly thought waiving him was a realistic possibility. But now that he’s back in the field, the likelihood of Richardson being waived is very slim. From talking to a few people behind the scenes on both sides, it appears that they’re trying to approach this situation amicably and professionally as his trade request looms over the franchise.
Keep in mind, waiving Richardson wouldn’t help the Colts financially since his contract is fully guaranteed as a former first-round pick. The only way the Colts could gain financial relief is if they trade Richardson. His market, however, is very dry, as evidenced by the team’s inability to trade him since his request became public in February. Now, I think his best chance of getting moved is if he has a solid showing in training camp — proving that he doesn’t have any lingering visual limitations from the orbital fracture he suffered in October — and if another team has a notable injury at QB. Perhaps that scenario would raise Richardson’s trade value and allow him to be shipped to a suddenly quarterback-needy team.
Assuming Richardson is not waived or traded, then it’ll be up to Colts coach Shane Steichen to reintegrate him into the team’s offensive plans because, clearly, Indy will have seen some value in keeping him around. Fans are fair to point out how dismissive Steichen comes off whenever he’s asked about Richardson, but the bottom line is that if Richardson is “here to compete,” as assistant general manager Ed Dodds recently said, then Steichen must hold up his end of the bargain and coach the 23-year-old he once advocated for the Colts to draft fourth in 2023.
Who starts at QB in Week 1? — @ClaytonClifford
Daniel Jones is the Colts’ unquestioned starter, so if he’s healthy enough, he’ll be QB1 in Week 1. His status, however, is understandably a bit unknown when considering that he’s around five months removed from rupturing his right Achilles tendon. But setting Jones aside for a second, I think the real question you’re asking is if Jones needs more time to rehab, then who’s starting in place of him in Week 1?
Right now, I’d lean toward Riley Leonard simply because the Colts have praised him all offseason as the presumed backup. Leonard, a 2025 sixth-round pick, started last year’s regular-season finale and showed promise in his brief stints as a rookie. But now that Richardson has returned, the Colts need to have a serious conversation about what Richardson’s presence really means. If he’s just here as a placeholder for the third-string spot behind Jones and Leonard, then he should be waived. It would be a waste of everyone’s time to bring him back and bury him on the depth chart with no real chance to elevate.
But since Leonard has barely played in the NFL, I don’t think he should simply be handed the backup job without a legitimate challenger this offseason. Therefore, the Colts should allow Richardson to compete for the QB2 role with Leonard and allow them to push each other. Both quarterbacks are young and flawed; however, at least this approach would promote the “competition” that Steichen and Colts general manager Chris Ballard are always preaching. Whoever wins would then be poised to start in Week 1 if Jones isn’t ready to go, and if Richardson can’t beat out Leonard to move up the depth chart, that would be quite the statement about his NFL future.
In your latest article, Dodds was the spokesperson after the rookie minicamp. Is this an effort to provide more opportunities for him as he has garnered interest from other teams? — Adam P.
Yes, the Colts have backed Dodds in his effort to land a general manager job. He’s interviewed for a handful of GM openings in recent years, including with the Tennessee Titans. But Dodds’ appearance during rookie minicamp wasn’t anything out of the ordinary or specifically designed to get him more face time. Per league rules, he’s required to speak with the media twice a year, and since I joined the Colts beat in 2022, Dodds has usually talked during training camp and at some point during spring practice. I actually thought he gave the most honest answer regarding Richardson’s status when he laid out that both sides must be mature about the QB’s failed trade request so far and work together as he enters the final year of his rookie deal.
Will Jonathan Taylor, DeForest Buckner, Josh Downs and Quenton Nelson get extensions as they enter contract years? — @LarryMooshaker
The only player you mentioned that I’d give a contract extension to is Nelson. The starting left guard is arguably the best offensive lineman in franchise history and will likely wear a gold jacket one day as a member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Nelson, 30, is a six-time Pro Bowler and hasn’t shown any signs of slowing down.
Taylor, Buckner and Downs, on the other hand, are more complicated. Taylor is coming off his third Pro Bowl nod in 2025, but it’s very rare for a running back to receive a third contract with the same franchise. Although Taylor, 27, didn’t miss a game last season, his injury history gives me pause. The same can be said for two-time All-Pro Buckner, 32, who underwent neck surgery at the end of last season. And with Downs, 24, I just don’t think he’s proven enough for the team to reward him with an extension. He’s coming off a career-low 566 receiving yards in 2025.
What’s the plan at receiver after not investing significant draft assets at the position? — Brad B.
The Colts appear to be content with using a committee to replace Michael Pittman Jr., who was traded to the Pittsburgh Steelers in March. So, I’d expect to see the team’s newly paid No. 1 receiver, Alec Pierce, and Downs receive a significant increase in targets. I also think the Colts can unlock tight end Tyler Warren even more after his impressive rookie campaign. If you’re looking for a clear-cut third receiver, though, the truth is the Colts don’t really have one, and from what I’ve gathered, they don’t plan to pursue one. Their third receiver will be some combination of free-agent veteran signee Nick Westbrook-Ikhine, veteran reserve and special teams ace Ashton Dulin and possibly rookie seventh-round pick Deion Burks, among others.
Are there any positions where the Colts are much better than they were last year? Cornerback, if healthy, is all I can reasonably say. — Steve F.
We’re in agreement on cornerbacks, even with Moore’s departure. Charvarius Ward Sr. and Sauce Gardner played just one full game together last year, and if they can stay healthy, they’re primed to be one of the better outside cornerback tandems in the NFL. Justin Walley, a 2025 third-round pick, continues to receive high praise from defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo. Walley missed his entire rookie season with a torn ACL, but he’s projected to be a better fit in Anarumo’s scheme than Moore was, from what I’ve been told.
I’d also argue that the Colts upgraded at safety and linebacker with the rookie additions of A.J. Haulcy and CJ Allen. Haulcy, a third-round pick out of LSU, offers more versatility on the back end than last year’s starting strong safety, Nick Cross, who joined the Washington Commanders in free agency. Allen, a second-round pick out of Georgia, will likely take over at middle linebacker for Zaire Franklin,…

The Kansas City Chiefs’ offseason is mostly complete.

full_text:
Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice will be under the spotlight again in 2026. Can he produce enough on the field and stay out of trouble off it to stick around Kansas City? Jason Miller / Getty Images
The Kansas City Chiefs’ offseason is mostly complete.
Rookie minicamp was last week, and the team will begin organized team activities later this month as it begins preparations for the 2026 season.
Before we move on, though, let’s take a quick look back. Here are some offseason winners and losers from the roster, based on moves the team made (or didn’t make) over the last few months.
I’m one of those who believed the Chiefs would look to address receiver during the early rounds of the NFL Draft. It seemed to make sense given the team’s uncertain future there, with Rashee Rice in the final year of his rookie contract and the team lacking depth behind its top three of Rice, Xavier Worthy and Tyquan Thornton.
And who knows? Perhaps if the draft had fallen a different way, the Chiefs would’ve taken a wideout with one of their three Day 2 picks.
As it stands, though, general manager Brett Veach appears to be putting his faith in Rice for 2026 while believing the receiver will avoid the off-field drama that marred his first three seasons.
Rice’s future is tough to predict. Because of injuries and suspension, he has played just 12 games in the last two years, though he’s maintained strong production when he has been out there.
Case in point: Rice averaged 2.16 yards per route run last season, according to TruMedia, which was 12th among 41 receivers with at least 50 receptions. He remains a perfect fit for the Chiefs offense thanks to his run-after-catch ability, with the team often using him on short throws while looking to maximize his physicality and strength.
Rice isn’t a complete receiver, but he has proved he can carry a heavy load. The Chiefs appear to be banking on him to do that again, while also giving him one more opportunity to show he can go a full calendar year without creating negative offseason headlines.
It’s up to Rice from here. That the Chiefs didn’t draft over the top of him leaves open the possibility that they could be interested in an extension past 2026.
His production — and behavior — will determine whether that comes to fruition, but the Chiefs have at least left open the path toward a longer future in K.C.
All-Pro defensive tackle Chris Jones was following the NFL Draft. And his early tweets over the weekend looked like this:
Jones hasn’t been one to make excuses for his play and is typically quick to take accountability when he messes up.
But I’m sure a question lingered in his mind through the past couple of seasons when he was mostly a one-person wrecking crew for the defensive line:
What if I just had a little more help?
We should find out now. The Chiefs went defense with their first four picks, which included adding a talented defensive tackle in first-rounder Peter Woods and a speed-rush specialist in second-rounder R Mason Thomas.
Both should aid Jones. His sack totals have been noticeably down the last two seasons (five in 2024, seven in 2025), even as his pressure numbers remained among the elite at his position.
Studies show that pressures are a better gauge than sacks for evaluating a pass rusher’s individual impact. But pressures also don’t produce the same results as getting a QB on the ground, and the Chiefs struggled to finish that job too often last season.
The hope now is that Jones will get a few more assists when he’s able to cause havoc in backfields.
A 2025 training camp knee injury put cornerback Kristian Fulton behind with the playbook , and the free-agent signee didn’t find his footing with the team until late in the season.
As a starter in the last two games, Fulton had four combined pass breakups against Denver and Las Vegas, showing glimpses of the potential the team hoped to see all season.
Now, though? It’s difficult to see how Fulton fits in after the Chiefs went heavy on cornerback in the draft.
K.C. moved up in the first round to take Mansoor Delane with the sixth pick , so he should be a starter right away. Second-year player Nohl Williams projects as the starter on the other side, and Veach also brought in 2022 first-round pick Kaiir Elam as a free agent to compete for an outside role.
Fulton doesn’t appear to have a clear path for playing time, which isn’t ideal for someone who is set to count $13 million against the 2026 salary cap. The Chiefs could still save $5 million by cutting him, or perhaps he’s still a trade candidate.
In any case, the offseason made it more difficult to envision him playing a large role in 2026.
An alpha competitor who projects as a starter despite his average size.
Tight end Travis Kelce turns 37 this season, so there was speculation Veach could look to find the potential Kelce replacement with a high pick in the draft.
That didn’t happen. The Chiefs, in fact, didn’t draft any tight ends, meaning they’ll be looking to lean on returners at the position while hoping they can produce more than in past years.
Backup Noah Gray had a down year by his standards and dealt with a late-season concussion in 2025. Beyond that, though, the Chiefs seem to be putting their faith in the oft-injured Jared Wiley, a 2024 fourth-round pick who has battled injuries each of his first two seasons.
As mentioned in last week’s Chiefs mailbag , Wiley displayed some blocking potential last season, with his best highlights coming during the Thanksgiving game against Dallas.
He needs to show more, though, to be considered a long-term solution for a position that will need reinforcements soon.
Linebacker Leo Chenal, who joined Washington in free agency this offseason, played 42 percent of the Chiefs’ defensive snaps last season even after missing the final three games with injury.
That’s a lot of playing time to fill, and the Chiefs didn’t add any free agent or draft pick who seems likely to replace that Chenal-sized hole in the roster.
It seems to mean the team will be asking a lot more from second-year player and former undrafted free agent Cooper McDonald.
The Chiefs already showed how much they valued McDonald when they protected him on their initial 53-man roster last season. And when linebacker Nick Bolton was asked this offseason about the team losing Chenal, McDonald was the first player he mentioned as someone who needed to step up.
K.C.’s third linebacker spot isn’t an every-game starter role, but it is a valuable piece, especially when facing opponents who are looking to establish dominance with their run game.
From their actions, the Chiefs appear to remain high on McDonald and his potential. It’s up to him now to prove that confidence warranted.
The Chiefs traded up in the seventh round to select running back Brashard Smith a year ago, but from the start, he appeared an awkward fit with their offense.
A former receiver, Smith showed an ability to catch but struggled to solidify a consistent role. Coach Andy Reid mentioned that he wanted Smith to add weight and muscle over the offseason to be better suited to handle a running-back load. Even as Kansas City failed to find any explosiveness with its 2025 run game, it didn’t turn to Smith for carries until a meaningless final-week game against Las Vegas.
The Chiefs gave themselves many more backfield options this offseason. They signed top-of-the-market running back Kenneth Walker III, added the versatile Emari Demercado in free agency, then moved up in the fifth round to draft shifty Nebraska running back Emmett Johnson. The team doesn’t have an obvious short-yardage option, so we can’t completely rule out a training-camp reunion with 30-year-old Kareem Hunt.
It all means Smith faces an important training camp. He’s a seventh-round pick, so the team doesn’t have a great amount invested in him if it does choose to move on.
Smith certainly will be one of the players we’ll be watching most closely when training camp begins in July.

title: Jordan James, Romello Height and 8 other young 49ers poised to break out in 2026 Backup tailback isn't always a marquee spot in San Francisco. However, Christian McCaffrey's age and usage might change that trend in 2026. Matt Barrows
summary:

The San Francisco 49ers’ under-25 club is becoming a bit more exclusive.

full_text:
Jordan James, a fifth-round pick a year ago, appears to be the early front-runner for the 49ers' No. 2 running back this season. Thearon W. Henderson / Getty Images
The San Francisco 49ers’ under-25 club is becoming a bit more exclusive.
Third-round pick Romello Height, for example, is already 25 after spending six seasons — at four schools — in college. Two other NFL Draft picks are 24, and undrafted rookie punter Jack Bouwmeester turned 27 earlier this month. That means he’s older than cornerback Deommodore Lenoir, a fifth-round pick in 2021.
Still, the 49ers have been trying to recapture their youth, with an 11-man draft class last year — every draftee remains on the roster — and an eight-man class last month.
Which of the team’s youngsters are best positioned to make a splash this season? To make the list, you have to be 25 or younger. And you can’t already have made an impact, which is why players such as Upton Stout (24) and Ricky Pearsall (25) aren’t included.
The list below ranks, in order, from most to least likely, a player’s chance of a breakout season in 2026.
James, a fifth-round pick a year ago, appears to be the early front-runner for the No. 2 running back this season. In some years, that hasn’t been a big deal in San Francisco. Last year’s backup, Brian Robinson Jr., logged a career-low 190 snaps.
This year, however, starter Christian McCaffrey is coming off a conspicuously heavy workload in 2025, and the 49ers consistently have said they want to give him more rest on game days.
“When you look around the league and you study great backs and study guys who affect the game like (McCaffrey) does, those guys do come out of the game,” offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said last week. “Those guys do get a blow sometimes, and whether it’s a drive or a couple plays in a series, it helps those players. Christian knows that, and we’ve got to do a better job as coaches, we’ve got to do a better job at times of getting a better rotation.”
Even if the 239-pound defensive end gets only pass-rush snaps as a rookie, he ought to see plenty of playing time. Outside of Nick Bosa, the 49ers don’t have any true pass-rush threats coming off the edge. Their other defensive ends — Mykel Williams, Sam Okuayinonu, Keion White and Cam Sample — combined for seven sacks last season. Unless the 49ers sign another Bosa brother, Height might already be their second-best edge rusher.
The 49ers are looking for a new slot or “F” receiver after Jauan Jennings signed with the Minnesota Vikings. Veteran Christian Kirk certainly is an option. His experience and speed give the team a chunk-play threat it hasn’t had in a while at the position.
Stribling, however, is far more Jennings-like in his ability to pancake opponents and otherwise help out in the running and short passing games. Coach Kyle Shanahan has cited a dip in downfield blocking as a factor in the 49ers’ lack of explosive runs and pass plays last season.
Stribling doesn’t have Jennings’ size or length, and he must build the kind of receiver-quarterback chemistry Jennings had with Brock Purdy in recent years. Still, Stribling is faster and offers big-play ability the 49ers were missing last season.
Several players will vie for the starting left guard position this offseason, including fourth-round pick Carver Willis and free-agent acquisitions Robert Jones and Brett Toth. Colby, however, might get the first crack at the job. He logged nearly 500 snaps there last season, and even though he wasn’t consistent enough to hold down the job, it might have served as a stepping stone for 2026. Colby invariably was the first name out of general manager John Lynch’s mouth when discussing the left guard competition this offseason.
Willis also seems to have a good shot at the left guard spot. He played in a similar system at Washington and is quick off the line of scrimmage, a prerequisite in the 49ers’ run game. The biggest issue: He only played tackle for the Huskies, and it’s hard to say how quickly he’ll pick up the new position in the NFL.
Make no mistake: Dre Greenlaw is the team’s designated weakside linebacker for 2026. Greenlaw, however, has appeared in only 10 games over the last two seasons and turns 29 later this month. Therefore, it’s hard to see him being a 17-game starter this season.
With Dee Winters now in Dallas, that likely leaves Martin, a third-round pick last year, as the first guy off the bench at the weakside spot. He’ll have to hold off rookie Jaden Dugger, and he’ll obviously have to remain healthy himself. Martin suffered a concussion on Nov. 30 and remained in the post-concussion protocol until the end of January. He’s been fully cleared and has been participating in the 49ers’ offseason program.
James’ biggest rival for the No. 2 running back spot might be Black, a third-rounder the 49ers thought was the second-best tailback in the recent draft. He’s not as elusive as James, but he is sharp and powerfully built, and he handles himself well as a backfield blocker. That last attribute won’t make Black popular in fantasy football circles, but it’s something a rookie needs to prove before he gets meaningful snaps.
Cowing was on this list last year, but he never played a snap because of a recurring hamstring issue he didn’t overcome until season’s end. Still, he might be the fastest player on the squad and is the early front-runner to handle punt-return duties in San Francisco, which he did as a rookie in 2024.
Watkins and Cowing seem to be competing for the same spot. Assuming Mike Evans, Pearsall, Stribling and Kirk are healthy when the season begins, that leaves one more receiver spot on the game day roster. Like Cowing, Watkins returns punts. He was off to a strong start last summer before a high-ankle sprain in the preseason opener knocked him to the bottom of the depth chart. Watkins is not as fast as Cowing, but he’s more thickly built and looked good on deep balls before he got hurt last summer.
Is the fifth-round pick a middle, weakside or strongside linebacker? The answer to that question: Yup. The uniquely sized Dugger — 6 feet 5, 242 pounds with 35-inch arms — was a middle linebacker at Louisiana, but he appears to have the skills to line up at any of the three spots.
Dugger’s level of competition at Georgetown (yes, the Hoyas have a football team) and Louisiana might make for a slow transition to the NFL. And the 49ers might be eying him mainly as a coverage ace on special teams this season.
Still, his new linebackers coach, K.J. Wright, was an enthusiastic advocate during the draft process, and Dugger seems custom-made for the strongside role that was problematic last season when opponents, especially the Los Angeles Rams, attacked the 49ers with tight-end-heavy sets.

title: Nobody’s Talking About the Cardinals’ Biggest Offseason Improvement
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals enter voluntary offseason activities this week with most of their roster constructed after massive talent acquisition periods from free agency and the draft.
Positions such as running back and quarterback stole the show in the desert this offseason, two of the more eye-catching spots for fans to recognize and discuss. While those players are obviously vital to an offense's success, much of the Cardinals' work along the line of scrimmage hasn't shared a similar spotlight.
And that's perhaps the most important upgrade the Cardinals have made this offseason.
Arizona's offensive line last season, for lack of better term, looked lost. The Cardinals' starting five was depleted by injuries and was under the watch of a rookie offensive line coach after coveted  coach Klayton Adams departed for the Dallas Cowboys.
Those factors, combined with overall poor team play, pinned Arizona's offensive line down to near the bottom of NFL rankings and rightfully so.
Fixing an offensive line isn't sexy. It's not making headlines, generating season ticket revenue or selling out jerseys by the fistful — yet for as much as the game of football changes, especially at the NFL level, the game is still won and lost within the trenches.
Arizona first began the upgrades in free agency, where the Cardinals made left guard Isaac Seumalo their top signing at a three-year, $31.5 million contract. Other faces in Matt Pryor, Oli Udoh and Elijah Wilkinson were signed (all with starting experience) with Wilkinson expected to be the guy at right tackle.
Work continued early in the draft, where Arizona used their second-round pick on guard Chase Bisontis , who is expected to eventually win the starting right guard position. The Cardinals also walked out of the draft with versatile tackle Jayden Williams.
Last season, the Cardinals' offensive line ranked near the bottom of the league in advanced stats such as yards averaged before contract on ball-carriers. While success is not promised, early signs of improvement are there for Arizona.
Take into account the below chart in Mike Clay's tweet, where Arizona's offensive line grades out as the 15th-best in the league.
Current 2026 NFL Offensive Line projected starters: pic.twitter.com/oGq7k4anGY
In one offseason, that's a strong turnaround. There's always going to be weak spots along an NFL roster — such is life. Right tackle isn't quite solidified in terms of stable play while we still need to see Bisontis both win the right guard job and execute to expectation.
With that being said, the Cardinals did do well in terms of effort to improve an offensive line that had quality guys in left tackle Paris Johnson Jr. and center Hjalte Froholdt already in store.
And if the Cardinals' offense does that take expected leap, fans will point to Jeremiyah Love or maybe even Carson Beck as a proponent of that success. While either or both could be the case, it's hard not to believe Arizona's quiet but strong effort in the trenches to add starters on top of key depth guys will have paid off, too.

title: Let's Slow Down The Carson Beck Hype Train Just a Tad
full_text:
ARIZONA – It feels like not even No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza is getting similar levels of hype to Arizona Cardinals quarterback Carson Beck.
Beck, a third-round draft choice, took the field alongside his fellow rookies for mini-camp with plenty of social media clips going viral.
Cardinals fans, like all other 31 fan-bases, are starved for actual football content to consume — but a clip of Beck moving around the pocket and throwing has stirred quite the interesting slew of conversations.
Such as Joe Burrow comparisons. In mini-camp. Wearing shorts and no helmet or pads. During a drill.
Carson Beck looks like Joe Burrow pic.twitter.com/TLR72qZLbr
The allure with Beck is certainly there. He's a 6-4 quarterback with plenty of college experience at two major programs with success at both Miami and Georgia. He worked in NFL-style offenses and is capable of being a game manager, especially with the talent around him in Arizona.
Yet it wasn't long ago when the Cardinals were heavily slandered on drafting Beck at the top of the third round, mostly by the same people claiming he'll be the starter and could acheive great heights.
Beck reminds me of a certain Bengals QB… 👀 pic.twitter.com/eQoqaeoOXv
And while that's certainly possible, we do need to shift this narrative back into perspective.
Jacoby Brissett is still very much projected to be the starting quarterback on opening day, even in spite of his absence from voluntary team activities in hopes of snagging a new contract.
While Beck will surely have an opportunity to prove himself in training camp, Brissett's the lead dog in that clubhouse for a reason.
"You want to be the guy out there. It's such an interesting position," Beck told reporters on potentially starting.
"It's why I think it's the best position on Earth. There's only one guy out there. ... So I mean obviously I would love to play and perform. But again, we'll see where that takes me and really just showing up and going to go to work."
Expectations for a third-round pick, especially quarterback, should always be tempered. That's not to say Beck isn't capable of contributing early — because he certainly is — though we also need to come back down to reality.
We're in May. Beck isn't going against live competition. Getting sucked into the world of hope from clips posted on social media is a recipe for dissapointment.
If Beck can carry momentum into training camp and preseason play, then this conversation should be had.
But even then, let's maybe stop the Burrow comps.

title: We Know Cardinals Won't Play These 6 Teams in Regular Season Opener
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals and their fans are eagerly awaiting the 2026 schedule release on Thursday, and as schedule leaks begin to creep into the public eye, we're slowly figuring out when and where some of the team's matchups will be.
So far, it's mostly been who the Cardinals won't play, at least in terms of their regular season opener.
The Cardinals have recently seen four teams eliminated from their regular season opener in the Kansas City Chiefs, Denver Broncos, Dallas Cowboys and New York Giants.
The Chiefs are set to play the Broncos on Monday Night Football while Sunday Night Football will see the Cowboys and Giants collide in Week 1.
With the Los Angeles Rams battling the San Francisco 49ers in Australia to begin the season, we can also cross out Arizona's two divisional rivals.
That's six teams we immediately know Arizona won't face in Week 1 — so who is left?
The Cardinals in theory could play on the road against the defending champion Seattle Seahawks, who will be playing the traditional first Thursday Night Football game to hang their championship banner and begin the new football season.
However, primetime execs probably don't want Arizona featured, so it feels like we can cross that probability out. The Cardinals are working under the first-year watch of head coach Mike LaFleur and Arizona is very much an unknown commodity at this point in time, which typically spells bad news for TV execs.
That leaves the Washington Commanders, Philadelphia Eagles, Las Vegas Raiders New York Jets, Detroit Lions, Los Angeles Chargers and New Orleans Saints as possible opponents.
Though we don't know exactly what the slate will look like, we do know Arizona's schedule will be vastly difficult. The Cardinals have, by two different metrics, one of the toughest schedules in the NFL when evaluating opponent win percentage and projected wins by Vegas.
Arizona has opened their regular season just once at home within the last six seasons — will that trend continue, or will the Cardinals play host at State Farm Stadium to begin the new year?
The Cardinals were previously featured in two primetime games last year, though Arizona may only get one or zero this coming season thanks to their low expectations. There's always a chance the Cardinals can get flexed into a primetime slot later in the season, however — which would be a good problem to have if you're Arizona.
The 2026 regular season schedule will be unveiled on Thursday. May 14 at 5:00 PM Arizona time.

title: The Cardinals’ Schedule Is So Ridiculous the Entire NFL Is Talking About It
full_text:
The NFL is set to fully release their 2026 regular season schedule on Thursday, and fans across the league have gotten a glimpse of the Arizona Cardinals' slate of opponents.
Despite finishing in fourth place in their division, the Cardinals have one of the toughest strengths of schedules in the NFL for 2026.
That's mostly due to being in a division with the Seattle Seahawks, Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers — though their out-of-division foes are incredible tough as well.
Congrats on the 1st pick in the 2027 NFL draft
"Fourth place schedule for the Cardinals... Welcome to hell," said one X user.
Using last year's win percentage for each opponent, the Cardinals have the third-toughest schedule in the league by that metric, trailing only the Chicago Bears and Miami Dolphins.
People on social media still believe Arizona has it worse.
I get it’s based off last years records but the Cardinals schedule is 100% harder https://t.co/D1iWo7wDXN pic.twitter.com/r9DFvp7c41
Outside of their division (where all three opponents made the postseason) the Cardinals will see playoff teams in the Denver Broncos, Philadelphia Eagles and Los Angeles Chargers while the Detroit Lions also had a winning record.
Like oh my god bro what could the Cardinals have possibly done to deserve this schedule😭😭😭 pic.twitter.com/jSUTXhZahF
That's perhaps the biggest argument for the Cardinals trying to climb their way out of the basement of the NFC West — the rest of the division is simply too good on a consistent basis for Arizona to keep tabs with.
No arguments/bragging/debates about SOS this year among the NFC West's elite. All grouped together in about the same bucket for schedule strength. Arizona having the toughest schedule after finishing 4th is odd, but it's OK because they got Carson Beck right? https://t.co/HXCubEXF2z
"Roger Goodell hates the existence of the Arizona Cardinals," said one X user while another responded with, "Damn what the cardinals do? lol that’s a rough schedule for sure. They don’t have a QB."
It's sure to be tough sledding for the Cardinals, especially with first-year head coach Mike LaFleur — who does have prior experience in the NFC West after spending time with the Rams and 49ers as an offensive coordinator.

"Everyone's got the same vision. And then you think about this division, it's a tough division. If it were easy, it wouldn't be worth it," LaFleur said on why he took the job in Arizona at his introductory press conference.
"We know the work that we got in front of us in the back right there [pointing to Cardinals players in attendance]. They know that. But those are the reasons I wanted to be the head coach here."

title: Actual NFL Cap Space Rankings: Where Cardinals Really Stand After Offseason
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals move into the final stages of the offseason with some spending power still in store.
The Cardinals are currently seventh in total NFL cap space rankings on OverTheCap with a $32.4 million figure, though that number will drop down as they sign more of their rookie class. However, looking at their effective cap space (which already factors in the money needed to sign their rookie class), Arizona still figures to be in good shape:
1. San Francisco 49ers ($66.4 million) 2. Tennessee Titans ($43 million) 3. Los Angeles Chargers ($40.4 million) 4. Washington Commanders ($36.9 million) 5. New England Patriots ($31.5 million) 6. Indianapolis Colts ($29.8 million) 7. Seattle Seahawks ($29.2 million) 8. Arizona Cardinals ($20.88 million) 9. Philadelphia Eagles ($20.87 million) 10. Los Angeles Rams ($20.86 million)
Teams typically like to carry around $5 million in "emergency" money throughout the regular season in case an unforeseen move is needed, though most organizations will likely elect to roll over the remaining camp into 2027.
That's the likely route for Arizona, where they're already projected to have a monster amount of cap space with a projected $140 million. Note: The Cardinals have several extension candidates to handle before then, so that number could change.
Still, Arizona will have some money to spread around in 2027 when they could potentially be in position to add a franchise quarterback in the draft. Of course that all depends on how events this season unfold, though that possibility is still there nonetheless.
The Cardinals didn't have a wild offseason in terms of spending, rather opting to make a few depth signings with Isaac Seumalo and Tyler Allgeier headlining their free agency class. Arizona was one of seven teams to sign 20 or more players in free agency though they ranked in the bottom half of the league when it comes to total money spent at $106.6 million.
Arizona, with high picks in every round, had one of the more expensive draft classes in the league. The Cardinals had no lower than the fourth overall selection in every round and didn't make any trades throughout the three day event.
That class is headlined by running back Jeremiyah Love and his fully guaranteed $53 million contract, which is doing a lot of the heavy lifting in Arizona's class in terms of financials.
Even with some expensive newcomers, the Cardinals still find themselves in great cap shape as training camp approaches.

title: Overlooked Draft Pick Could Actually Be Cardinals Instant Impact Rookie
full_text:
Names such as Jeremiyah Love and Carson Beck headline the Arizona Cardinals' 2026 draft class, and with both featuring at their prominent positions of running back and quarterback, that's expected.
However, second-round pick Chase Bisontis could end up being a top contributor.
Bisontis is projected to compete (and honestly win) the job at right guard after being made the 34th overall pick.
ESPN's Field Yates had Bisontis as one of his greatest impact rookies:
"It should not be surprising that the second pick of Day 2 is expected to have a legitimate early role. However, I'm particularly enthused by Bisontis' short-term outlook because of Arizona's needs on the right side of its line. While I fully expect Bisontis to settle in as the starting right guard, his experience as a right tackle as a freshman at Texas A&M indicates that he has the necessary versatility to play significant snaps immediately."
Offensive linemen never get the proper credit they deserve and they'll never sell jerseys, though Bisontis could be a massive puzzle piece to Arizona's offensive line.
Yates brings up a good possibility of Bisontis potentially being an option at right tackle this offseason as well. The right side of the line was unsure at both guard and tackle entering the draft, though Bisontis is considered likely to slot in at guard (over Isaiah Adams) as opposed to tackle over Elijah Wilkinson.
"Yeah, it wasn’t that difficult. It took a couple of spring practices—felt comfortable," Bisontis said on his versatility switching between right tackle and left guard.
"Like I said, mean, tough and nasty and that’s what it is (for an) interior offensive linemen. I felt really comfortable there. I loved it. I’m willing to do anything the team needs. If they need me to snap (or) play tackle, I’m there.”
Love will be sharing carries in a stacked backfield with Tyler Allgeier and James Conner while Beck will be competing for a starting spot with veteran quarterbacks in Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew.
Bisontis has strong capability to impact both the rushing and passing attack, as he arrives to Arizona as a path-creator for running backs while not allowing a sack in pass protection in his final 18 college games.
If he can live up to his potential, Bisontis legitimately might be Arizona's biggest impact rookie — and even with more prominent names in his class, that wouldn't be a bad thing.

title: What Carson Beck Said on Competing for Cardinals QB Job
full_text:
ARIZONA — Third-round picks are always interesting.
Carson Beck wasn't a top selection in the draft, stalling some expectations of starting immediately for the Arizona Cardinals while he wasn't quite a late draft pick either with no reasoning to immediately contribute.
Yet as the Cardinals' offseason marches on, Beck's draft position has somewhat of undefined expectations for his 2026 role due to a few reasons.
Third-round picks are right in that purgatory of simply being an unknown commodity. The current status of Cardinals veteran quarterback Jacoby Brissett also opens a potential door for Beck to start if contract demands aren't met.
But also from a talent perspective, there's a path for Beck to compete for a starting job in training camp, even if he's not expected to win it.
"I think for me the most important thing is get in the building. I started meeting with the coaches and going over the playbook and learning the guys around me," Beck said when asked about the path to starting. He'd also have to bypass Kedon Slovis and Gardner Minshew in the process.
"Build relationships, start to connect with them, be myself, and then just go play ball. Have fun, enjoy the process. But again, I just try to improve and get better each and every day. And if I continue to do that, I think we'll see where that takes me."
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur made it seem like Arizona would keep the door open for a quarterback competition in training camp despite reports of Brissett being the QB1 for 2026.
Arizona's been adamant they're not placing immediate pressure on Beck to earn a starting role with general manager Monti Ossenfort telling reporters he simply wanted Beck to just know where the cafeteria was when he got to the Cardinals facility.
Beck's hoping to eat on the field, too — but isn't in a rush to stuff his plate and won't be mad if he's forced to wait.
"Each and every day will be a learning experience. Even if I were to be the guy at some point, you are consistently and constantly learning just through game experience, through practice experience, meetings just talking to guys around the facility, right? Just trying to get all the little breadcrumbs that I can from each and every person," said Beck.
"But again, everybody wants to play football, especially at the position of quarterback. You want to be the guy out there. It's such an interesting position. It's why I think it's the best position on Earth. There's only one guy out there. ...  So I mean obviously I would love to play and perform. But again, we'll see where that takes me and really just showing up and going to go to work."

title: These 13 Cardinals Are Still Free Agents
full_text:
The Arizona Cardinals are likely done making massive offseason changes to their roster after supplementing talent and depth across events such as free agency and the draft.
As a result, the Cardinals still have a handful of previous players sitting in free agency. Ten Cardinals from last season went and found new homes. While there's sure to be a few more moves involving former Arizona players, the following names are still available on the open market:
Williams was paid a two-year, $30 million contract to anchor down the Cardinals' right side of the line before a slew of injuries prevented him from playing for majority of the two seasons he was here in the desert.
Jones/Nichols arrived here in the 2024 offseason along with Williams and were hoping to provide the Cardinals' defensive line with a veteran boost — though both suffered injuries and were largely unavailable for their stint in the desert.
Beachum was a pivotal swing tackle that filled in when needed, mostly at right tackle when Williams was hurt through the last couple of years. He was fairly steady in the Cardinals' lineup and could be eying retirement.
The same could be said for Jones, who operated as Arizona's WR3 when healthy. He didn't get much run time in the Cardinals' offense ran by coordinator Drew Petzing and he just simply wasn't impactful enough to warrant bringing back.
Hernandez was well loved across the locker room and was a nasty guard when healthy, though consecutive years with season-ending knee injuries prevented him from continuing his strong form pre-2024.
Special teams players in Brewer/Haack were fine in their respective roles, though Arizona decided it was time to move on from the long-time long snapper in Brewer while typical starting punter Blake Gillikin was re-signed this offseason.
The rest of the crew in Brown, Deguara, Baccellia, Russell and Vokolek were simply role players in Arizona, though Baccellia was a tenured practice squad effort player while Vokolek was a key blocking tight end after Tip Reiman went down to injury last offseason.
Arizona has a projected $20.8 million in effective cap space, per OverTheCap. They're close to the 90-man offseason roster limit.
